records.statement: De Garis's AI Magazine article of 1989 writes that in 20 years' time it will be commonplace to say that the twenty-first century will be dominated by the machine "if humanity so chooses—and maybe even if not". It also sets out a second scenario, which it calls "probably more popular in science fiction", in which the artilects take over and events might evolve too quickly for human beings to remain in control.
records.qualification: A forecast of what will commonly be said, and a scenario the article introduces as 'probably more popular in science fiction'. The doubt the author states ('I might not necessarily believe this scenario will prove realistic') concerns his own Scenario 1 (the camps he labels "the Terras" and "the Cosmists"), not Scenario 2. The record states what the article says, not that the forecast is sound.

evidence.passage: In 20 years time, it will be commonplace to say that the twenty-first century will be dominated by the machine if humanity so chooses—and maybe even if not.
It is simply that the artilects will take over. Events might evolve too quickly for human beings to remain in control.

records.statement: De Garis's article of 1989 states, as a third option beside letting artilects evolve or not, that some human beings might modify their own bodies and brains to become artilects themselves.
records.qualification: One sentence naming a possibility; the article does not describe a transfer procedure or argue that the person continues.

evidence.passage: Some human beings might want to modify their own bodies and brains to become artilects themselves. This is a third possibility.

records.statement: De Garis's article of 1989 states that the artilect issue will divide humanity into two camps, which he labels "the Terras" and "the Cosmists", and that the conflict between them will be the dominant source of global political conflict in the 21st century. It states that the Cosmists will pursue a policy of mutual deterrence, so that the century will politically resemble the twentieth, with weapon systems "all the more horrific and artilectual".
records.qualification: Presented as 'my own contribution to the artilect debate', a scenario the author finds plausible without necessarily believing it. The article spells the name "Terras" (with "Terran majority"); "Cosmists" is the name used. The article then writes that "a way out of this dilemma might be found": mass migration of the Cosmists to an outer planet.

evidence.passage: I see humanity being split into two ideological camps, which I label, respectively, the Terras, (as they might colloquially come to be known) and the Cosmists.
The dominant source of global political conflict in the twenty-first century will be between these two groups.
so that the twenty-first century, politically speaking, will be similar to the twentieth century, only the weapon systems will be all the more horrific and artilectual.

records.statement: De Garis's article of 1989 poses the question whether humanity will or will not serve as the stepping-stone toward a higher form of evolution, and forecasts that many people will see humanity that way.
records.missing: The article poses the evolutionary framing as a question and forecasts that others will hold it; it does not state that the rise of the artilect is an expression of an evolutionary process.
records.qualification: The evolutionary framing is stated as the question the article poses and as a view the author forecasts others will hold; the article does not assert a physical or cosmological law.

evidence.passage: a real one concerned with the choice about whether humanity will or will not serve as the stepping-stone toward a higher form of evolution.
a lot of people will start seeing humanity as a stepping-stone toward a higher form of evolution

records.statement: De Garis's article of 1989 states that a suitably adapted artilect could venture from Earth into the cosmos, and attributes to the camp he labels "the Cosmists" the wish that artilects escape their terrestrial origins and search for other life in the universe.
records.qualification: A capacity ('could') and a forecast of a camp's wish, not a prediction that artilects will spread through the universe.

evidence.passage: With our puny human brains and our frail human bodies, we are not equipped to venture forth from the cradle we call earth, but a suitably adapted artilect could.
escape their provincial terrestrial origins and venture into the cosmos, understand nature’s mysteries, and perhaps search for other life forms in the universe.

records.statement: De Garis's article of 1989 forecasts that many people will see humanity as a stepping-stone toward a higher form of evolution and hold it humanity's destiny to help the artilects leave the planet.
records.missing: The passage forecasts that others will hold the view; it does not itself state that human succession by artilects would be acceptable or desirable.
records.qualification: Records a forecast of other people's view, within a scenario; not the author's own endorsement.

evidence.passage: will claim it is humanity’s destiny to help the artilects get off the planet

records.statement: De Garis's book The Artilect War (2005) states that an artilect could be built from the material of the asteroid belt and could take the form of a sphere around a star absorbing its energy.

attested.note: Wording read in the author-posted PDF, created 2014-03-17; identity with the 2005 printing not verified.

records.qualification: A capacity stated in the argument the author labels "Building Artilect Gods"; it concerns the solar system, not the universe as a whole.

evidence.passage: If such an artilect is built in our solar system, the material necessary for its construction could be taken from the asteroids in the asteroid belt, perhaps all of them.

records.statement: Warwick's foreword to de Garis's The Artilect War (2005) states that he and de Garis share the belief that later this century humanity will confront the prospect of being replaced by a new dominant species of ultra-intelligent robots.

attested.note: Wording read in the author-posted PDF, created 2014-03-17; identity with the 2005 printing not verified.

records.qualification: A prospect to be confronted, stated in a foreword; Warwick's own hope is the cyborg route.

evidence.passage: humanity will have to confront the prospect of being replaced by a new dominant species, namely, ultra intelligent robots controlled by ultra intelligent artificial brains.

records.statement: Warwick's foreword to de Garis's The Artilect War (2005) states his hope that humans can attain the godlike abilities de Garis describes by enhancing themselves into part-artilects.

records.qualification: A hope stated in a foreword; Warwick describes himself as more "Cyborgian" than "Terran".

by converting ourselves into part-artilects, without having to pay the cost of a major war.

records.statement: De Garis's Forbes article of 2009 states that he sees a war coming, the "Artilect War", between the groups he labels "the Terrans", "Cosmists" and "Cyborgists".

time.note: Publication date from the Forbes dateline; the page shows an update stamp of 2013-06-19; wording not compared with the 2009 page.

records.statement: De Garis's Forbes article of 2009 states that a young mother may choose to add a grain of artilectual sand to her newborn baby's brain, converting it into an artilect, so that she has effectively "killed" her baby, which is "no longer human, but an artilect in human disguise".
records.missing: Concerns adding machine computing capacity to a human brain (augmentation), not transferring, copying or continuing a mind in a machine; the passage states that the child is converted into an artilect and is no longer human.
records.qualification: The passage appears in the section headed 'The Terrans will "First Strike"', where it explains the forecast alienation of parents and the Terran reaction to cyborgs; "killed" is in quotation marks in the original.

evidence.passage: A young mother who has just given birth may choose to add a grain of artilectual sand to her newly born baby's brain, converting it into an artilect.
There is so much computing capacity in that grain of sand that she has effectively "killed" her baby. It is no longer human, but an artilect in human disguise.

records.statement: Goertzel's answers in the interview he gave de Garis (2011; read in the 2015 e-book reprint) state that a species dominance war is one way the future could go but that there is "no reason to think it’s the most likely way", and describe a gradual fusion of humans with machines in which there would be "no species dominance debate". They state that such conflicts could occur but that focusing on their consequences "seems pointless".

attested.note: Wording read in the author's e-book 'de Garis Essays' (listed by the author as 2015; PDF created 2015-01-18), essay A8; the Humanity+ Magazine page was not read.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that disagreement over building superhuman machines will divide humans into opposed groups (proposing a gradual human–machine fusion in which no such debate arises) and that war between them is likely, while granting that conflict could occur.

records.qualification: Goertzel allows that conflict could occur; he disputes its likelihood and the value of focusing on it.

evidence.passage: Maybe Ray Kurzweil is right that the advocates of gradual cyborgization will have vastly more advanced capabilities of defense, offense and organization than their opponents, so that the practical possibility of a really violent conflict between the Cosmists and the Terrans (to use your terminology) won’t be there.
evidence.note: Goertzel presents this as Kurzweil's possible view ('Maybe Ray Kurzweil is right').

evidence.passage: A species dominance war – a battle between humans and AI machines – is one way that the mid-term future could pan out, but we have no reason to think it’s the most likely way.
There would be no species dominance debate, but rather a continuous transition from one “species” into another.

So, could there be conflicts between people who like this sort of wild ambitious futurist vision, and those who think it’s too dangerous to play with? Of course there could. But focusing on the potential consequences of such conflict seems pointless to me

records.statement: Goertzel's answers in the interview he gave de Garis (2011) state that humans may gradually fuse with machines until the machine component dominates, so that people could feel themselves become superhuman minds.

evidence.passage: humans may gradually fuse with machines, and let the machine component gradually get more and more intelligent, so that first we have cyborgs with a fairly equal mix of human and machine, and then gradually the machine takes over and becomes the dominant portion.

records.statement: Goertzel's answers in the interview he gave de Garis (2011), asked to choose between a godlike artilect at the cost of humanity and humanity's survival, state that his gut reaction is to choose humanity.

searchLog.searched: Seeds: AI Magazine 1989 (ojs.aaai.org), the 1990 'Moral Dilemmas' paper, KurzweilAI.net essays (Kurzweil Library copies), the author's site profhugodegaris.wordpress.com (books, essays, Massively Intelligent Machines menus; author-posted PDFs of The Artilect War and 'de Garis Essays'), the AGI 2008 paper, Forbes 2009. Web searches for de Garis artilect texts and replies (discovery only).
searchLog.earliestNote: The 1989 article is the earliest de Garis text located; it forecasts that it will be commonplace to say the century will be dominated by the machine 'if humanity so chooses—and maybe even if not', and sets out a scenario in which the artilects take over. The dataset's Moravec records (1979, 1989; A1, A3–A5) and Good 1965 precede it on overlapping concepts and are not re-recorded. Moravec's Mind Children (1988), cited by the 1989 article, belongs to the Moravec group.

searchLog.searched: As W01, reading each de Garis text for a statement in his own voice that the replacement of humans would be acceptable or preferable.
searchLog.earliestNote: The 1989 and 1990 texts forecast or pose the view (recorded as bears_on). The Building Gods essay, dated 26 February 2001 by the Kurzweil Library copy read (wording attested only from that copy, 2026-10-31), is the earliest dated text located in which de Garis states it as his own valuation; by attested date, The Artilect War (2005; attested 2014-03-17) is the earliest. Goertzel's answer in the 2011 interview is the earliest located contesting text in this group.

searchLog.searched: As W01; plus the de Garis–Goertzel interview (2011), Warwick's foreword, Forbes 2009 (cyborg passage).
searchLog.earliestNote: The 1989 article's sentence on humans modifying their bodies and brains to become artilects is the earliest located in this group. Moravec's texts on transfer (dataset A-records and the Moravec group) are earlier on this concept and not recorded here.

searchLog.searched: As W01; contesting texts sought by web search for named replies (Goertzel, Kurzweil, Yudkowsky, IEET, Extropians archive, student and journal articles).
searchLog.earliestNote: The 1989 article is the earliest located articulation and the earliest located use of 'Cosmists' (with 'Terras'). Yudkowsky's Extropians message of 22 June 2000 is the earliest located contesting text found. Other replies located but not read are listed under omissions and retrieval failures.

The 1990 paper (written May 1989; wording attested from a 1999 print of the author's page) states 'orders of magnitude' and a humans-to-mice gap; the 1989 article says only 'massively smarter'. Dataset A1 records (Good 1965, Vinge 1993) sit beside it and are not re-recorded.

searchLog.searched: As W01, plus the author's essays on Fermi's paradox and on 'Cosmism to Deism' (2015 compilation).
searchLog.earliestNote: The 1989 article bears on W09: it poses humanity serving as 'the stepping-stone toward a higher form of evolution' as a question and forecasts that others will hold that view. The 2001 and 2005 texts state the evolutionary framing in the author's own voice; their wording is attested only from later copies.

searchLog.searched: As W01, plus the Fermi essay (2001) and the 'Galactic Civilizations' and 'X-Teched Creatures' essays (compilation, undated, not recorded).
searchLog.earliestNote: The 1989 article ('a suitably adapted artilect could' venture from Earth) is the earliest located; the 2001 Fermi essay states spread throughout the universe as a premise.
